newsitem.title: USA: Republican turmoil may cost them in next election.
newsitem.headline: Republican turmoil may cost them in next election.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent
Republicans, in turmoil after last week's failed attempt to depose House Speaker Newt Gingrich, are beginning to wonder if their internal disarray could hurt them in next year's mid-term elections.

Under normal circumstances, Republicans should anticipate a banner year in 1998. The party holding the White House has lost seats in every mid-term with the sole exception of 1934 and losses are particularly heavy, averaging some 40 House seats, in the sixth year of a presidency.
However, some Republican lawmakers and commentators are so worried about the fighting within their party they are predicting far smaller gains next year, or worse.

"Off-year elections are about turnout. If Republican voters out there are kind of disillusioned ... turnout could drop by 2 or 3 percent. That's all it would take," said Bill Kristol, the Republican editor of the conservative Weekly Standard magazine.
"Democrats could retake the House. I don't think that's out of the question," he said.

Republicans enjoy a narrow 12-seat majority in the 435-member House of Representatives. But 21 of their members won election in 1996 with less than 51 percent of the vote and are obviously vulnerable.
Republican control of the Senate in 1998 is not seen as being under threat and the party could even widen its 55-45 majority because several Democrats in Republican-leaning states are retiring.

Fear of the election was part of the reason for the revolt against Gingrich, who remains highly unpopular in the nation. Conservatives, who are the heart of the uprising, are frustrated at the effortless way President Bill Clinton seems able to outmanoeuvre their leadership time and again.
The collapse of the revolt solved neither of these problems and merely intensified distrust and intrigue permeating the party, which seems set for more of internal strife in the months ahead.
Gingrich seems traumatized by his strategic defeat at Clinton's hands in 1995, when Republicans were blamed for shutting down the federal government.

He was further weakened earlier this year when he was reprimanded and fined by the House for ethical violations. Now, he finds himself squeezed between the president on one side and his own members on the other in crucial budget and tax negotiations with the White House.

"Republicans have lost the public relations battle. They have been unable to craft a message and compete politically with Clinton, who has seized the political centre," said American University political scientist Allan Lichtman.
"Clinton is suddenly the champion of the middle class and Republicans are defenders of the rich. They might as well paint their Achilles heel with fluorescent paint," he said.
With Gingrich running scared, Republicans looked to Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott and their new party chairman Jim Nicholson to fill the leadership void. Both have disappointed.
Lott has been unwilling or unable to become a high profile public spokesman while Nicholson has remained a gray, anonymous figure, unknown to the country at large.
"I don't think we have a leader right now," said Tony Blankley, Gingrich's former spokesman.

Tensions between Republicans who stress economic issues and those for whom social questions are uppermost have grown, as demonstrated by the refusal of Senate Foreign Relations chairman Jesse Helms to allow Massachusetts Gov. William Weld, a fellow Republican, to become U.S. ambassador to Mexico.
For all the bad news, the good news for Republicans is that the 1998 elections remain 15 months away -- an eternity in politics.

"Ninety-nine percent of the American people do not care about 99 percent of the news that comes from Washington about all this intrigue," said New York Representative Bill Paxon, who was forced to resign his position in the Republican House leadership following the coup attempt.
But Paxon conceded his party still had a problem.
"We are not communicating the great work of our members, and we're not doing it in an effective way," he said.
